title: Umrah and Hajj
hook: the lesser pilgrimage any time, the greater in Dhul Hijjah

segments.voice: Yesterday, istita'ah, being able, and your line: once, if able. What did you find you could do now that you once couldn't? Day one thousand one hundred twenty.

Two travel bookings to Mecca. One is for a week in early spring, the dates picked to fit a school break. The other is for a fixed handful of days in a fixed month, booked through an agency with a waiting list, and it can't be moved by a single day. Both travelers will put on white. Both will walk around the Kaaba. One is going on umrah. The other is going on Hajj. From the outside they can look almost the same. They aren't. Today, umrah.
screen: `TWO BOOKINGS TO MECCA.` → `ONE MOVABLE, ONE FIXED.` → `ALMOST THE SAME, BUT NOT.`

segments.voice: First, the verse that names both. Surah two of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "Perform the pilgrimage and the visit (to Mecca) for Allah." The pilgrimage is Hajj. The visit is umrah. Two acts, named side by side, both for Allah. Second, when. Umrah can be made at any time of the year. Hajj has its own days in its own month, Dhul Hijjah, and outside those days there is no Hajj. That's why one booking moves and the other doesn't. Third, what's inside. Umrah is short: entering the pilgrim's state, ihram; walking around the Kaaba, the tawaf; walking between the hills of Safa and Marwah; and cutting or shaving the hair. Hajj holds those rites and adds more: the standing at Arafah we met this week, the night at Muzdalifah, the days at Mina. Fourth, lesser and greater. The Qur'an, in surah nine, speaks of "the day of the Greater Pilgrimage." Some scholars read that phrase as setting Hajj beside a lesser pilgrimage, the umrah. Lesser doesn't mean worthless. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says one umrah to the next wipes away what falls between them, and an accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise. And the schools differ on how binding umrah is. The Shafi'i and Hanbali schools hold it a duty once in a life for those able. The Hanafi and Maliki schools hold it a strongly recommended practice. Each gives its reasons. One more thing for the end of the week. The week opened with two special fasts, Arafah and Ashura, which took us from the edge of the year to its start. Then a hidden night, a short line asking pardon, a fast kept safely, two joys, and a door marked if able. Today, two pilgrimages, one lesser and one greater.
screen: `THE PILGRIMAGE AND THE VISIT.` · `ANY TIME, OR ONE MONTH.` · `A FEW RITES, OR MANY.` · `THE DAY OF THE GREATER PILGRIMAGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn the difference, by heart. Settle, and breathe. Say it to yourself slowly. Umrah: any time of year. Ihram, the walk around the Kaaba, the walk between two hills, the cut of the hair. Hajj: only in Dhul Hijjah. All of that, and Arafah, and Muzdalifah, and Mina. Go back over it once more without hurrying. If you know someone who has made either journey, picture their face and think of asking them about it. The bell holds the time.
Umrah. The visit, the lesser pilgrimage to Mecca, which can be made any time of year, set beside Hajj in surah two. Today's word.
Your line: lesser and greater. Today, if someone you know has been to Mecca, ask which journey it was and what they remember. Tomorrow: the boundary. Day one thousand one hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Muslims make umrah at any time of year, sometimes more than once, and make Hajj in Dhul Hijjah on its set days; some combine the two in one journey during the Hajj season.
